questions.q: An email says 'Your account is locked — click here now to fix it.' Best move?
options: Click fast before it's too late
Stop, don't click, and verify via the official site or IT
Forward it to the whole team
questions.explain: Urgency + a link to 'fix' your account is the classic phishing pattern. Navigate to the real site yourself or check with IT.

questions.q: What's the strongest single habit for account safety?
options: Writing passwords on a sticky note
questions.explain: Unique passwords (a manager helps) and MFA mean one leaked password doesn't open everything.

questions.q: The 'CEO' texts you urgently asking for gift cards. This is most likely:
questions.explain: Urgency, secrecy, and an odd payment method are textbook impersonation. Verify through a known channel before acting.

questions.q: Best defence against ransomware wiping your work?
options: Tested, offline backups and prompt patching
questions.explain: Reliable backups let you recover without paying, and patching closes the holes ransomware exploits.

questions.q: You find a USB stick in the car park. You should:
options: Plug it in to find the owner
Hand it to IT/security and never plug it in
questions.explain: 'Lost' USB drives are a known attack. Plugging in unknown devices can auto-install malware — hand it to security.

questions.q: Good rule for sensitive data and public AI or web tools?
options: Never paste secrets/customer data into unapproved tools
questions.explain: Treat any external tool like sending data outside the building. Use approved tools and keep secrets out of public ones.

chains.title: Handling a suspicious email
steps: Notice the urgency or odd request
Don't click any links or attachments
Verify the sender via a known channel
